newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Local police take over in divided Mostar.
newsitem.headline: Local police take over in divided Mostar.

text.p: International authorities handed over police powers in Mostar to local officers on Tuesday, raising law-and-order concerns for the Bosnian city deeply divided between Moslem and Croat communities.
Western European Union police formally ended their responsibility for policing in Mostar, scene of some of the bitterest fighting between the two ethnic rivals up until two and a half years ago.
Since the fighting ended, intense divisions have remained between Moslem east Mostar and the Croat-controlled west.
Western Mostar has become notorious as a gangster city whose mafia rulers oppose reintegration as bad for their "business".
Up to 70 members of the United Nations International Police Task Force will remain in an advisory role until the Moslem- Croat federation in Bosnia forms an integrated police force.
In the meantime, Moslem and Croat officers will share police duties, U.N. officials said.

The international community, which applied fierce pressure to force the two reluctant groups into forming the city's joint governing bodies, wants their leaders to assume full responsibility for Mostar's destiny.

Local authorities have so far failed to agree on a police chief, raising fears that joint operations may have some difficulty in getting off the ground. Administative structures and pay are also unresolved.
Local police minister Valentin Coric told Reuters: "In the next couple of days we will name the head of the Mostar police and it is not very important if he is a Croat or a Moslem."
Residents of the divided city, where fighting raged for 11 bitter months in 1993 and 1994, were not so sure.
Anto, a 37-year-old Croat from west Mostar, said: "We should stay separated and take care of our own business. It will be just a formality."

Emir, a 24-year-old Moslem police officer from the eastern sector of the city, remarked: "You know who doesn't want peace. We will have it formally, but we'll have our Moslem patrols here on our side and theirs on their side."
The deputy secretary general of the WEU, Horst Holthott, also struck a cautious note at the handover ceremony.
"The WEU police have acted as a catalyst. Now the catalyst has come to the end of its mission. The united force of Mostar must ensure sufficient momentum to continue under its own auspices," he said.
